**Surat al-'Asr** (the chapter of "The Declining Day")

It is Meccan according to Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Zubayr and the majority of scholars, and Medinan according to Mujahid, Qatadah and Muqatil. Its verses number three, without disagreement. Despite its brevity, it gathers a great deal of the sciences (ʿulūm) of the Qur'an. It is related from al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, that he said: "If nothing had been revealed other than this surah, it would have sufficed people, for it encompasses all the sciences of the Qur'an."

al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat* and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* narrated from Abu Hudhayfah, who had companionship with the Prophet, that he said: "When two men from the Companions of the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, met, they would not part until one of them recited the surah *Wa'l-'Asr* to the other, and then one of them would greet the other with peace." In it there is an allusion to the state of one whom abundance (al-takathur) has not distracted, and for this reason it was placed after the surah of *al-Takathur*.

**In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.**

﴿By the time﴾. Muqatil said: God, glorified is He, swore by the prayer of 'Asr (ʿAṣr, the afternoon prayer) because of its excellence, since according to the majority it is the *al-Salat al-Wusta* (the middle prayer), on account of the saying of the Prophet, upon him be peace: "They have kept us busy from the middle prayer, the prayer of 'Asr."

And [this is] because of what is in the codex (muṣḥaf) of Hafsah: "And the middle prayer is the prayer of 'Asr."

And in a hadith: "Whoever misses the prayer of 'Asr, it is as if he has been robbed of his family and his property."

It is related that "a woman used to cry out in the alleys of Medina: 'Point me to the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him!' He, upon him be peace, saw her and asked her: 'What has happened?'

She said: 'O Messenger of God, my husband went away, so I committed fornication, and a child was born to me from that fornication. I threw the child into a jar of vinegar and it died, then I sold that vinegar. Is there any repentance for me?' He, upon him be peace, said: 'As for fornication, upon you is stoning because of it. As for killing, its recompense is Hell. As for selling the vinegar, you have committed a grave sin. But I think you had abandoned the prayer of 'Asr.'"

This was mentioned by the Imam [al-Zamakhshari], and by my life, he is an imam in transmitting such things, which are not relied upon by the scholars of hadith. So beware of following him in this.

The prayer was singled out for excellence because performing it is more difficult, since people are busy at the end of the day with their trades, their earnings and their livelihoods.

It was also said: God, mighty and majestic, swore by the time of that prayer, because of the excellence of its prayer, or because of the creation of Adam, father of mankind, upon him be peace, in it, on a Friday. Qatadah followed this view; it is related from him that he said: "'Asr is al-'ashiyy (the late afternoon/evening)." God, glorified is He, swore by it as He swore by *al-Duha* (the forenoon), because of the signs of power in both of them.

al-Zajjaj said: "*al-'Asr* is the day, and *al-'Asr* is the night," and upon this is the verse of Humayd ibn Thawr:

*"The two 'asrs (day and night) did not tarry, a day and a night, when they sought to overtake whatever they aimed at."*

It was also said: "*al-'Asr* is the morning (bukrah) and *al-'Asr* is the evening (ʿashiyyah)"; these are the two coolings (al-ibrādān). Upon this view, and upon what precedes it, the oath is by one of the two matters without specifying which.

It was also said: the intended meaning is the 'Asr of prophethood (ʿaṣr al-nubuwwah), as if He meant the time of his life, upon him be peace, as if it were the most noble of eras, to honor the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him.

It was also said: it is the time of his life, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, and what follows it until the Day of Resurrection; and its measure, in what has passed of time, is the measure of the time of 'Asr in the day. This is indicated by what al-Bukhari narrated from Salim ibn 'Abd Allah, from his father, that he heard the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, say: "Your remaining (bāqā'ukum) in comparison with those nations before you is only like what is between the 'Asr prayer and the setting of the sun."

Its nobility is due to its being the time of the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, and of his community, which is "the best community brought forth for mankind." Its being late does not harm it, just as a spear-point's lateness from the tips of its shaft does not harm it, nor the blossom's lateness from the tips of its branches.

Ibn 'Abbas said: it is *al-Dahr* (the age, the eternal time). God, mighty and majestic, swore by it because it comprises kinds of wonders; for this reason it is called "Abu'l-'Ajab" (father of wonder). It is as if God, exalted is He, reminds by the oath by it of what is in it of blessings and their opposites, to alert the human being who is prepared for loss and for happiness. God, mighty and majestic, also alludes, by the oath by it, to its magnification by negating that it could have any loss or any role in what happens, as one who attributes events to it claims. And the attribution of loss to mankind after this oath indicates that it is a quality of mankind, not of time, as is said:

*"They blame time, though there is in it no faults belonging to time; the faults are those of people unworthy of time."*

It has been criticized that the use of *al-'Asr* in this sense is not apparent.

Indeed, mankind is in loss (khusr).

That is, a loss in their trades and endeavours, and in spending their lives on their aims, from which they gain nothing in the Hereafter; rather, these may even harm them when they arrive at the Sahirah (the wakeful land, i.e., the place of resurrection).

The definite article in al-insan is for comprehensiveness (al-istighraq, i.e., encompassing all of mankind), as indicated by the exception that follows. The indefinite noun khusr is said to be for magnification, meaning a great loss. It may also be for specification (al-tanwi'), meaning a kind of loss different from what man recognises.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 103, verse 3:

﴿Except those who have believed and done righteous deeds﴾: indeed they are in a trade that will never fail, for they have sold the perishing, base thing and bought the enduring, precious thing. They have exchanged the enduring righteous deeds for the transient morning and evening goods. How wonderful is this transaction, how profitable! And how clear is this benefit, which comprises all good!

The intended meaning of the relative pronoun is everyone who is characterised by the description in the relative clause, not only ʿAli, may God honour his face, and Salman al-Farisi, may God be pleased with him, as one might imagine from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, mentioning only them. Rather, they are included in this at the first level of inclusion. Similarly, his restricting the "man who is in loss" to Abu Jahl is evident. This is an explanation of their perfecting of themselves.

God the Exalted's words: ﴿and they enjoined one another to the truth﴾, etc., are an explanation of their perfecting of others. That is, some of them enjoined others to the established matter, which cannot be denied and whose good effects never cease in either abode, namely all good, from faith in God, Mighty and Majestic, and following His books and His messengers, peace be upon them, in every belief and action.

﴿And they enjoined one another to patience﴾: patience against the sins to which the soul yearns by the disposition of human nature, and patience in the acts of obedience which are difficult for it to perform, and patience in the face of the calamities with which God the Exalted tests His servants. The patience mentioned is included within the truth, but it is mentioned after it with the repetition of the preposition and of the verb to which it is attached, to show the utmost care for it. It is also possible that the first refers to the rank of worship, which is doing what pleases God the Exalted, and the second refers to the rank of servitude, which is contentment with what God the Exalted has done. For the meaning of patience is not merely restraining the soul from what it craves, whether an action or an abstention; rather, it is receiving what comes from Him, Mighty and Majestic, with graciousness and being content with it, inwardly and outwardly.

Sallam, Harun, and Ibn Musa reported from Abu ʿAmr: «wal-ʿaṣir» with a kasra on the ṣad, and «waṣ-ṣabir» with a kasra on the bāʾ. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "This is not permissible except in pausal position, with transfer of the vowel" (naql al-ḥaraka). It was also narrated from Abu ʿAmr «biṣ-ṣabir» with a kasra on the bāʾ as ishmam (a partial, lip-rounded vowel). As he said, this too is only in pausal position. The author of al-Lawami' said: "ʿĪsa of Basra read «biṣ-ṣabir» with the vowel of the rāʾ transferred to the bāʾ, so that one would not need to pronounce a fragment of a vowel in pause, nor to make it sukun so that two consonants come together. This is a widespread dialect, not an anomalous one; rather it is common. It indicates the i'rab (grammatical inflection) and separates the meeting of two sakins, and fulfils the right of the word on which one pauses, from the sukun." End of quotation.

From this, as in al-Bahr, is his saying:

"I am Jarir, my kunya is Abu ʿAmr; I strike with the sword, and Saʿd is in the ʿaṣir."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and others reported from ʿAli, may God honour his face, that he used to recite:

«By the time, and the calamities of the age, indeed man is in loss, and indeed he is in it until the end of the age».

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Dawud in the Masahif reported from Maymun ibn Mihran that he recited: «By the time, indeed man is in loss, and indeed he is in it until the end of the age, except those who have believed». He mentioned that this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud.

Some of the Mu'tazilites argued from what is in this surah that the perpetrator of a major sin is eternal in the Fire, because it made no exception from loss except "those who have believed and done righteous deeds", etc. It was answered that there is no indication in this beyond the fact that the one not excepted is in loss. As for his being eternal in the Fire, there is no indication of that at all. Loss is general: it is either by eternity, if he dies as a disbeliever, or by entering the Fire, if he dies as a sinner; and it does not preclude the forfeiting of the lofty ranks if He forgives him. This is a good answer. Al-Shaykh al-Maturidi, may God have mercy on him, had elaborate and forced explanations regarding this in his Ta'wilat, which are mentioned there, so do not overlook them. In the surah there is also an exhortation to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and that a person should love for his brother what he loves for himself, which is well known.
